questions.stem: An ideal gas goes through the cycle shown, from A to B to C to D and back to A. What is the net work done by the gas during one cycle?
questions.explanation: The net work done by the gas is the area enclosed by the cycle: \((3\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3)(3\times 10^5\text{ Pa})=900\text{ J}\). It is positive because the cycle runs clockwise. The area under A to B alone is \(1200\text{ J}\).

questions.stem: For the process from A to B in the cycle shown, what is the work \(W\) done on the gas?
questions.explanation: At constant pressure, the work done on the gas is \(W=-P\Delta V=-(4\times 10^5)(3\times 10^{-3})=-1200\text{ J}\). The gas expands, so it does positive work on its surroundings and the work done on it is negative.

questions.stem: During the process from B to C in the cycle shown, which statement about the gas is correct?
choices: The gas does work, and heat is added to the gas.
No work is done, and heat is added to the gas.
The temperature stays constant, because the volume is constant.
No work is done, and the gas transfers energy to its surroundings as heat as its temperature falls.
questions.explanation: The volume does not change, so \(W=0\). The pressure falls at constant volume, so \(PV\) and the temperature fall, and \(\Delta U<0\). By \(\Delta U=Q+W\), \(Q\) must be negative.

questions.stem: For the cycle shown, the temperature of the gas at state D is \(300\text{ K}\). What is the temperature at state B?
questions.explanation: For a fixed amount of gas, \(T\) is proportional to \(PV\). At D, \(PV=1\times 1\) in the graph's units; at B it is \(4\times 4=16\). So \(T_B=16(300)=4800\text{ K}\). States A and C are each at \(1200\text{ K}\).

figure.alt: Pressure versus volume graph of a cycle for an ideal gas. A is at 1 × 10⁻³ m³ and 4 × 10⁵ Pa; B is at 4 × 10⁻³ m³ and 4 × 10⁵ Pa; C is at 4 × 10⁻³ m³ and 1 × 10⁵ Pa; D is at 1 × 10⁻³ m³ and 1 × 10⁵ Pa. The gas goes from A to B to C to D and back to A

questions.stem: For one complete cycle shown, how does the net energy added to the gas as heat compare with the net work done by the gas?
choices: The heat added is greater, because some energy is stored as internal energy each cycle.
They are equal, because the gas returns to its initial state and its internal energy does not change.
The work done is greater, because the gas does work in every process.
The heat added is zero, because the cycle is closed.
questions.explanation: Internal energy depends only on the state of the gas, so \(\Delta U=0\) over a cycle. Then \(Q=-W\): the net heat added equals the net work done by the gas, the enclosed area.

figure.alt: Pressure versus volume graph showing two expansions of an ideal gas from the same starting state to three times the starting volume. Curve 1 falls less steeply and ends at a higher pressure; curve 2 falls more steeply and ends at a lower pressure

questions.stem: An ideal gas expands from the same starting state to the same final volume in two ways, shown by curves 1 and 2. One process is isothermal and the other is adiabatic. Which curve represents the adiabatic process, and why?
choices: Curve 1, because an adiabatic process keeps the temperature constant.
Curve 2, because more heat enters the gas during that process.
Curve 1, because the pressure falls more slowly when no heat is exchanged.
Curve 2, because with no heat entering, the gas uses internal energy to do work, so its temperature and pressure fall further.
questions.explanation: In an isothermal expansion, heat enters to keep the temperature constant, so \(PV\) stays fixed. In an adiabatic expansion, \(Q=0\) and the work done by the gas lowers its internal energy and temperature, so it ends at a lower pressure.

figure.alt: Pressure versus volume graph showing two expansions of an ideal gas from the same starting state to three times the starting volume. Curve 1 falls less steeply and ends at a higher pressure; curve 2 falls more steeply and ends at a lower pressure

questions.stem: For the two expansions shown, how does the work done by the gas compare?
choices: More work is done by the gas in process 1, because the area under its curve is greater.
More work is done in process 2, because its pressure changes more.
The work is the same, because the change in volume is the same.
No work is done in process 1, because the temperature is constant.
questions.explanation: The work done by a gas is the area under the curve on a pressure–volume diagram. Curve 1 lies above curve 2 at every volume, so it encloses more area.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of \(2.0\text{ mol}\) of an ideal gas at \(300\text{ K}\) in a \(0.050\text{ m}^3\) container? Use \(R=8.31\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\).
questions.explanation: \(P=\dfrac{nRT}{V}=\dfrac{2.0(8.31)(300)}{0.050}\approx 1.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\), about atmospheric pressure. Omitting the division by volume gives about \(5.0\times 10^3\).

questions.stem: Hydrogen molecules (molar mass \(2\text{ g/mol}\)) and oxygen molecules (molar mass \(32\text{ g/mol}\)) are in the same container at the same temperature. What is the ratio of the root-mean-square speed of the hydrogen molecules to that of the oxygen molecules?
questions.explanation: The molecules have the same average kinetic energy, \(\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\), so \(v_{\text{rms}}\) is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\). The mass ratio is 16, so the speed ratio is 4.

questions.stem: The absolute temperature of an ideal gas is increased from \(300\text{ K}\) to \(1200\text{ K}\). By what factor does the root-mean-square speed of its molecules change?
choices: It increases by a factor of 16.
questions.explanation: The root-mean-square speed is proportional to \(\sqrt{T}\). Multiplying the absolute temperature by 4 multiplies the speed by 2, while the average kinetic energy quadruples.

figure.alt: Distributions of molecular speeds for two samples of the same gas. Gas X peaks at about 400 m/s with a tall, narrow curve. Gas Y peaks at about 700 m/s with a shorter, broader curve that extends to higher speeds

questions.stem: The graph shows the distributions of molecular speeds in two samples of the same gas. Which sample is at the higher temperature?
choices: Gas X, because its peak is taller
Gas Y, because its distribution is shifted toward higher speeds
Gas X, because more of its molecules move at the most probable speed
They are at the same temperature, because they are the same gas
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy, which shifts the distribution toward higher speeds and spreads it out. The peak must then be lower so that the total number of molecules is unchanged.

figure.alt: Distributions of molecular speeds for two samples of the same gas. Gas X peaks at about 400 m/s with a tall, narrow curve. Gas Y peaks at about 700 m/s with a shorter, broader curve that extends to higher speeds

questions.stem: In the graph, the areas under the two curves are equal. What does this indicate about the samples?
choices: They contain the same number of molecules.
They are at the same temperature.
They have the same average speed.
They have the same internal energy.
questions.explanation: The area under a distribution counts all of the molecules in the sample. The shapes differ because of temperature; equal areas mean equal numbers of molecules.

questions.stem: What is the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at \(300\text{ K}\)? Use \(k_B=1.38\times 10^{-23}\text{ J/K}\).
questions.explanation: \(\overline{K}=\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT=1.5(1.38\times 10^{-23})(300)\approx 6.2\times 10^{-21}\text{ J}\). It depends only on temperature, not on the kind of molecule. Using \(k_BT\) alone gives \(4.1\times 10^{-21}\).

questions.stem: A gas absorbs \(500\text{ J}\) of heat while it does \(200\text{ J}\) of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.explanation: Work done by the gas is \(200\text{ J}\), so the work done on the gas is \(W=-200\text{ J}\). Then \(\Delta U=Q+W=500-200=300\text{ J}\).

questions.stem: A gas in an insulated cylinder is quickly compressed by a piston, so that no heat is exchanged. What happens to its temperature?
choices: It stays the same, because no heat enters the gas.
It decreases, because the gas loses energy to the piston.
It stays the same, because the pressure increases to compensate.
It increases, because the work done on the gas increases its internal energy.
questions.explanation: With \(Q=0\), the first law gives \(\Delta U=W\), and \(W>0\) when the gas is compressed. The internal energy of an ideal gas is proportional to its temperature, so the temperature rises, as in a diesel engine.

questions.stem: Heat flows by conduction through a flat wall. The wall's thickness and its area are both doubled, and the temperatures on the two sides are unchanged. How does the rate of heat flow change?
questions.explanation: The rate of conduction is \(\dfrac{kA\Delta T}{L}\). Doubling the area doubles it and doubling the thickness halves it, so the two changes cancel.

questions.stem: A glass window has an area of \(2.0\text{ m}^2\), a thickness of \(4.0\text{ mm}\), and a thermal conductivity of \(0.80\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}\). The temperature difference across it is \(20\text{ K}\). At what rate does heat flow through it?
questions.explanation: \(P=\dfrac{kA\Delta T}{L}=\dfrac{0.80(2.0)(20)}{0.0040}=8.0\times 10^3\text{ W}\). Forgetting to convert millimeters to meters gives \(8.0\text{ W}\).

questions.stem: A copper block at \(80^\circ\text{C}\) is placed in contact with an aluminum block at \(20^\circ\text{C}\) in an insulated container. Which statement describes the final state?
choices: Both blocks reach the same internal energy.
Heat continues to flow until both blocks reach \(50^\circ\text{C}\), regardless of their masses.
Heat flows from the block with more internal energy to the block with less.
Both blocks reach the same temperature, though they need not have the same internal energy.
questions.explanation: Heat flows from higher to lower temperature until the temperatures are equal. The final temperature and each block's internal energy depend on the masses and specific heats.

questions.stem: Which process would violate the second law of thermodynamics?
choices: Heat flowing on its own from a cold object to a hot object, with no other change
A gas expanding freely into a vacuum
Ice melting in a warm room
A refrigerator using electrical work to move heat from its cold interior to a warm kitchen
questions.explanation: The second law requires that the total entropy of an isolated system never decrease. Heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot; a refrigerator does so only because work is done on it, which increases entropy elsewhere.

questions.stem: The heat engine shown takes in \(1000\text{ J}\) from the hot reservoir and releases \(700\text{ J}\) to the cold reservoir in each cycle. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: The work done is \(Q_H-Q_C=300\text{ J}\), and the efficiency is \(\dfrac{W}{Q_H}=\dfrac{300}{1000}=30\%\). The ratio \(\dfrac{300}{700}\) compares work with the waste heat, not with the input.

questions.stem: The reservoirs of the engine shown are at \(600\text{ K}\) and \(300\text{ K}\). What is the greatest efficiency the engine could possibly have?
questions.explanation: The maximum, or Carnot, efficiency is \(1-\dfrac{T_C}{T_H}=1-\dfrac{300}{600}=50\%\). Real engines are less efficient because of friction and other irreversible processes.

questions.stem: An inventor claims that an engine like the one shown can convert all of the heat it takes in into work, with \(Q_C=0\). Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
choices: It is possible, because it conserves energy.
It is impossible, because it violates the first law of thermodynamics.
It is impossible, because it violates the second law of thermodynamics.
It is possible if the cold reservoir is at \(0^\circ\text{C}\).
questions.explanation: Such an engine would conserve energy, so it does not violate the first law. The second law, however, requires that some heat be released to a colder reservoir; the Carnot efficiency is less than 100 percent for any \(T_C>0\text{ K}\).

questions.stem: A gas at a constant pressure of \(2.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\) expands from \(1.0\text{ L}\) to \(3.0\text{ L}\). How much work does the gas do on its surroundings? \((1\text{ L}=1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3)\)
questions.explanation: The work done by the gas is \(P\Delta V=(2.0\times 10^5)(2.0\times 10^{-3})=400\text{ J}\). Multiplying by the final volume gives \(600\text{ J}\), and omitting the conversion from liters gives the large value.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container of gas is at \(27^\circ\text{C}\) and pressure \(P\). It is heated to \(327^\circ\text{C}\). What is the new pressure?
questions.explanation: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. The temperature goes from \(300\text{ K}\) to \(600\text{ K}\), so the pressure doubles. Using Celsius temperatures gives the incorrect factor of 12.

questions.stem: When a gas expands adiabatically, its temperature decreases. Which statement best explains why?
choices: The molecules spread out, and spreading out lowers the temperature directly.
Heat flows out of the gas as it expands.
The gas does work on its surroundings using its own internal energy, because no heat enters to replace it.
The pressure stays constant, so the temperature must fall.
questions.explanation: With \(Q=0\), \(\Delta U=W\), and \(W<0\) when the gas expands. The lost internal energy means lower average molecular kinetic energy and a lower temperature.

questions.stem: Helium and nitrogen gases are in the same container at the same temperature. Which statement is correct?
choices: Their molecules have the same average kinetic energy, and the helium atoms move faster on average.
Their molecules have the same average speed.
The nitrogen molecules have more average kinetic energy, because they are more massive.
The helium atoms have more average kinetic energy, because they move faster.
questions.explanation: Temperature sets the average translational kinetic energy, \(\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\), for every ideal gas. Lighter molecules must therefore move faster to have the same kinetic energy.

questions.stem: An ideal gas does \(800\text{ J}\) of work on its surroundings while its temperature stays constant. What is the heat transferred to the gas?
questions.explanation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so \(\Delta U=0\). With \(W=-800\text{ J}\) of work done on the gas, \(Q=\Delta U-W=+800\text{ J}\): heat enters the gas.

questions.stem: A hot gas and a cold gas are separated by a thin metal wall. Which statement best describes how energy is transferred between them at the molecular level?
choices: Heat particles travel through the wall from the hot gas to the cold gas.
Faster molecules of the hot gas collide with the wall and transfer kinetic energy that the wall passes on to the slower molecules of the cold gas.
Molecules of the hot gas pass through the wall into the cold gas.
The cold gas transfers its coldness to the hot gas through the wall.
questions.explanation: Conduction is energy passed by collisions. On average, collisions transfer kinetic energy from faster to slower particles, so energy moves from the hot side to the cold side until the average kinetic energies are equal.

questions.stem: \(0.20\text{ kg}\) of water at \(80^\circ\text{C}\) is mixed in an insulated container with \(0.60\text{ kg}\) of water at \(20^\circ\text{C}\). What is the final temperature?
questions.explanation: The heat lost by the hot water equals the heat gained by the cold water: \(0.20(80-T)=0.60(T-20)\), which gives \(T=35^\circ\text{C}\). The result is closer to the temperature of the larger mass.

questions.stem: Charges \(+4Q\) and \(-Q\) are fixed on the \(x\)-axis as shown. At what position, other than at infinity, is the electric field zero?
questions.explanation: The field can vanish only where the two fields point in opposite directions and the weaker charge is closer, which is to the right of \(-Q\). At a distance \(s\) beyond \(-Q\), \(\dfrac{4}{(d+s)^2}=\dfrac{1}{s^2}\), so \(2s=d+s\) and \(s=d\).

figure.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 120" width="360" height="120" role="img" aria-label="A charge of +4Q at x = 0 and a charge of −Q at x = d on the x-axis" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="10" y1="70" x2="350" y2="70" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="60" y1="66" x2="60" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="150" y1="66" x2="150" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="240" y1="66" x2="240" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="330" y1="66" x2="330" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="60" y="96" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">0</text><text x="150" y="96" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">d</text><text x="240" y="96" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">2d</text><text x="330" y="96" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">3d</text><circle cx="60" cy="70" r="14" stroke="#ec4899" stroke-width="1.8" fill="#ec4899"/><text x="60" y="75" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-size="10">+4Q</text><circle cx="150" cy="70" r="11" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="150" y="75" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-size="10">−Q</text><text x="346" y="62" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">x</text></svg>
figure.alt: A charge of +4Q at x = 0 and a charge of −Q at x = d on the x-axis

questions.stem: Why can the electric field not be zero at any point between the two charges shown?
choices: Between them the fields of both charges point in the same direction, toward the negative charge.
The fields there are too strong to cancel.
The field is always zero only at the midpoint between two charges.
Electric fields cannot be added between charges.
questions.explanation: The field of \(+4Q\) points away from it, to the right, and the field of \(-Q\) points toward it, also to the right. Fields in the same direction add, so they cannot cancel there.

questions.stem: Two point charges exert an electric force of magnitude \(F\) on each other. Both charges are doubled and the distance between them is tripled. What is the new magnitude of the force?
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law gives \(F\propto\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\). Doubling both charges multiplies the force by 4, and tripling the distance divides it by 9.

questions.stem: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of \(100\text{ V}\). What kinetic energy does it gain? Use \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
questions.explanation: The work done by the field is \(|q|\Delta V=(1.6\times 10^{-19})(100)=1.6\times 10^{-17}\text{ J}\), or \(100\text{ eV}\). The electron gains this energy by moving toward higher potential.

\(5.0\text{ V/m}\), directed toward the \(10\text{ V}\) line
\(500\text{ V/m}\), directed toward the \(10\text{ V}\) line

choices: Toward A, the region of higher potential
Toward B, the region of lower potential
It remains at rest, because the potential there is not zero
questions.explanation: The field points toward lower potential, and the force on a negative charge is opposite the field. Electrons accelerate toward higher potential, losing electric potential energy as they gain kinetic energy.

questions.stem: A charge is moved at constant speed along one of the dashed lines in the diagram. How much work does the electric field do on it?
choices: A positive amount, because the charge moves.
A negative amount, because work is needed to move it.
None, because the potential is the same everywhere on the line.
It depends on the sign of the charge.
questions.explanation: The work done by the field is \(-q\Delta V\), and \(\Delta V=0\) along an equipotential. The field is perpendicular to the equipotential line, so it has no component along the displacement.

questions.stem: Three charges are placed on a line as shown. What are the magnitude and direction of the net electric force on the charge on the right?
questions.explanation: The middle charge attracts it with \(\dfrac{kq^2}{d^2}\) to the left, and the left charge repels it with \(\dfrac{kq^2}{4d^2}\) to the right. The net force is \(\dfrac{3kq^2}{4d^2}\) to the left.

questions.stem: For the arrangement shown, which statement about the middle charge is correct?
choices: The net force on it is zero, and it returns to its position if displaced along the line.
The net force on it points toward the right charge.
It is pulled toward the left charge, because that charge is listed first.
The net force on it is zero, but if it is displaced slightly along the line, it is pulled farther from its starting point.
questions.explanation: The two attractive forces are equal and opposite. If the middle charge moves toward one neighbor, that attraction grows and the other weakens, so the equilibrium is unstable along the line.

questions.explanation: The capacitance \(C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\) is halved, and the battery keeps the voltage fixed, so \(Q=CV\) is halved. Charge flows back to the battery.

questions.stem: The capacitor shown is charged and then disconnected from the battery. The plates are then pulled farther apart. What happens to the charge, the potential difference, and the field between the plates?
choices: The charge decreases, the potential difference stays the same, and the field decreases.
The charge stays the same, the potential difference increases, and the field stays the same.
The charge stays the same, and the potential difference and the field both decrease.
questions.explanation: An isolated capacitor keeps its charge. The field between the plates depends on the charge per unit area, which is unchanged, and the potential difference is \(Ed\), which increases with the separation.

questions.stem: How much energy is stored in a \(2.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) capacitor charged to \(10\text{ V}\)?
questions.explanation: \(U=\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2=\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0\times 10^{-6})(10)^2=1.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ J}\). Leaving out the factor of one half gives \(2.0\times 10^{-4}\).

questions.explanation: Between parallel plates the field is uniform with \(E=\dfrac{\Delta V}{d}=\dfrac{12}{0.0030}=4.0\times 10^3\text{ V/m}\).

questions.stem: A dielectric with dielectric constant 3 is slid between the plates of the capacitor shown while it remains connected to the battery. What happens to the charge on the plates?
choices: It is reduced to one third.
It increases by a factor of 9.
questions.explanation: The dielectric multiplies the capacitance by 3. With the battery holding the voltage fixed, \(Q=CV\) also triples.

figure.alt: Graph of electric field magnitude versus distance r from the center of a charged conducting sphere of radius R. The field is zero for r < R, jumps to its largest value at r = R, and decreases as 1/r² outside

questions.stem: The graph shows the electric field around a charged, solid conducting sphere of radius \(R\). Which statement explains why the field is zero inside the sphere?
choices: The sphere contains no charge at all.
The charges inside the sphere cancel only at the center.
The metal blocks electric field lines from entering.
The excess charge resides on the surface, and charges inside a conductor rearrange until the internal field is zero.
questions.explanation: Free charges in a conductor move until no force acts on them, which requires zero field inside. The excess charge spreads over the surface, and outside the field is that of a point charge at the center.

figure.alt: Graph of electric field magnitude versus distance r from the center of a charged conducting sphere of radius R. The field is zero for r < R, jumps to its largest value at r = R, and decreases as 1/r² outside

questions.stem: For the charged conducting sphere whose field is graphed, how does the electric potential inside the sphere compare with the potential at its surface?
choices: It is the same everywhere inside and equal to the surface potential.
questions.explanation: Because the field inside is zero, no work is done moving a charge within the conductor, so the potential cannot change from point to point. A zero field means a constant potential, not a zero potential.

questions.skill: Electric potential of a point charge
questions.stem: What is the electric potential \(0.30\text{ m}\) from a point charge of \(+2.0\text{ nC}\)? Use \(k=9.0\times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{/C}^2\).
questions.explanation: \(V=\dfrac{kq}{r}=\dfrac{(9.0\times 10^9)(2.0\times 10^{-9})}{0.30}=60\text{ V}\). Dividing by \(r^2\) gives the field, \(200\text{ N/C}\), not the potential.

questions.stem: How much work must be done to bring a \(+1.0\text{ }\mu\text{C}\) charge from very far away to a point \(0.20\text{ m}\) from a fixed \(+4.0\text{ }\mu\text{C}\) charge? Use \(k=9.0\times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{/C}^2\).
questions.explanation: The work equals the increase in electric potential energy, \(\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}=\dfrac{(9.0\times 10^9)(4.0\times 10^{-6})(1.0\times 10^{-6})}{0.20}=0.18\text{ J}\). Dividing by \(r^2\) gives \(0.90\).

questions.stem: At the midpoint between a \(+q\) charge and a \(-q\) charge, which statement is correct?
choices: The electric field is zero, but the potential is not zero.
Both the potential and the field are zero.
The potential is zero, but the electric field is not zero.
Neither the potential nor the field is zero.
questions.explanation: Potential is a scalar, and the contributions \(\dfrac{kq}{r}\) and \(\dfrac{-kq}{r}\) cancel. Field is a vector, and both fields point toward the negative charge, so they add.

questions.stem: A negatively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere, without touching it. The sphere is briefly connected to the ground, the ground connection is removed, and then the rod is taken away. What is the final charge on the sphere?
choices: Positive on the side nearer the rod and negative on the far side, with zero net charge
questions.explanation: The rod repels electrons, some of which flow to the ground. Breaking the ground connection before removing the rod traps the deficit of electrons, leaving the sphere with a net positive charge.

questions.stem: A balloon rubbed on hair becomes negatively charged and sticks to a neutral wall. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The wall becomes positively charged by gaining protons from the air.
Gravity holds the balloon against the wall.
The negative charge on the balloon is attracted by the neutral wall's net positive charge.
The balloon polarizes molecules in the wall, so the positive ends are slightly closer to the balloon than the negative ends and the attraction outweighs the repulsion.
questions.explanation: The wall's net charge stays zero. Its charges shift slightly, and because the electric force weakens with distance, the attraction to the nearer positive ends is stronger than the repulsion from the farther negative ends.

questions.skill: Motion of charges in a uniform field
questions.stem: What is the magnitude of the acceleration of an electron in a uniform electric field of \(1000\text{ N/C}\)? Use \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) and \(m_e=9.11\times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\).
questions.explanation: \(a=\dfrac{eE}{m_e}=\dfrac{(1.6\times 10^{-19})(1000)}{9.11\times 10^{-31}}\approx 1.8\times 10^{14}\text{ m/s}^2\). The electron's tiny mass makes gravity negligible by comparison.

questions.stem: A proton starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of \(500\text{ V}\). What is its final speed? Use \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) and \(m_p=1.67\times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\).
questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives \(qV=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), so \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(1.6\times 10^{-19})(500)}{1.67\times 10^{-27}}}\approx 3.1\times 10^5\text{ m/s}\). The value \(9.6\times 10^{10}\) is \(v^2\).

questions.stem: An oil drop of mass \(1.6\times 10^{-15}\text{ kg}\) is held motionless between horizontal plates by an upward electric force in a field of \(1.0\times 10^5\text{ N/C}\). Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), how many excess elementary charges does the drop carry? Use \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
questions.explanation: Balancing forces gives \(q=\dfrac{mg}{E}=\dfrac{(1.6\times 10^{-15})(10)}{1.0\times 10^5}=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\), exactly one elementary charge. Millikan found that every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of this value.

questions.stem: Why can two electric field lines never cross?
choices: At any point the electric field has a single direction, and crossing lines would indicate two directions at the same point.
Field lines repel each other because they carry charge.
Field lines always run parallel to each other.
Field lines cross only at the location of a charge.
questions.explanation: A field line is drawn tangent to the net field at every point. Because the net field at a point is a single vector, only one line can pass through it.

questions.stem: A \(3.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) capacitor and a \(6.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) capacitor are connected in series. What is their equivalent capacitance?
questions.explanation: For capacitors in series, \(\dfrac{1}{C}=\dfrac{1}{3.0}+\dfrac{1}{6.0}=\dfrac{1}{2.0}\). Series capacitance is less than either capacitor, the reverse of resistors in series.

questions.stem: A \(3.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) capacitor and a \(6.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) capacitor are connected in parallel across a \(12\text{ V}\) battery. What is the charge on the \(6.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) capacitor?
questions.explanation: In parallel, each capacitor has the full \(12\text{ V}\) across it, so \(Q=CV=(6.0\times 10^{-6})(12)=72\text{ }\mu\text{C}\). The total charge on both is \(108\text{ }\mu\text{C}\).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates electric field lines to equipotential surfaces?
choices: Field lines are parallel to equipotential surfaces.
Field lines point toward higher potential.
Field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces and point toward lower potential.
Field lines and equipotential surfaces are unrelated.
questions.explanation: Moving along an equipotential surface requires no work, so the field has no component along it. The field points in the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, the battery has no internal resistance. What is the current through the battery?
questions.explanation: The parallel pair has resistance \(\dfrac{6.0(3.0)}{6.0+3.0}=2.0\text{ }\Omega\), so the total is \(4.0\text{ }\Omega\) and the current is \(\dfrac{12}{4.0}=3.0\text{ A}\). Adding all three resistors as if in series gives \(1.1\text{ A}\).

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, what is the current through \(R_3\)?
questions.explanation: The \(3.0\text{ A}\) battery current produces \(6.0\text{ V}\) across \(R_1\), leaving \(6.0\text{ V}\) across the parallel pair. The current through \(R_3\) is \(\dfrac{6.0}{3.0}=2.0\text{ A}\), and through \(R_2\) it is \(1.0\text{ A}\).

questions.explanation: \(P=I^2R=(3.0)^2(2.0)=18\text{ W}\). The battery supplies \(36\text{ W}\) in all.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, \(R_2\) is removed, leaving an open gap where it was. How do the current through the battery and the potential difference across \(R_3\) change?
choices: The battery current decreases, and the potential difference across \(R_3\) increases.
The battery current increases, and the potential difference across \(R_3\) decreases.
questions.explanation: Removing a parallel branch raises the total resistance to \(5.0\text{ }\Omega\), so the battery current falls to \(2.4\text{ A}\). Less current means less voltage across \(R_1\) (\(4.8\text{ V}\)), leaving \(7.2\text{ V}\) across \(R_3\).

questions.stem: The three bulbs shown are identical. How do their brightnesses compare?
choices: Bulbs B and C are brightest, and bulb A is dimmest.
Bulb A is dimmest, because current is used up by the time it returns.
Bulb A is brightest, and bulbs B and C are equally bright.
questions.explanation: All of the battery's current passes through A and then divides equally between B and C. Each of B and C carries half of A's current and dissipates one quarter of A's power.

choices: A becomes dimmer, and B becomes brighter.
A becomes brighter, and B stays the same.
questions.explanation: With C removed, A and B are in series, so the total resistance rises from \(1.5R\) to \(2R\) and the current through A falls. B now carries the whole current, which is more than the half share it had before, and its voltage rises from one third to one half of the battery's.

questions.stem: Each bulb shown has resistance \(R\), and the battery has emf \(\varepsilon\) and no internal resistance. What is the power dissipated by bulb A?
questions.explanation: The total resistance is \(R+\dfrac{R}{2}=\dfrac{3R}{2}\), so the current through A is \(\dfrac{2\varepsilon}{3R}\). Then \(P=I^2R=\dfrac{4\varepsilon^2}{9R}\).

questions.stem: The switch in the circuit shown is closed. Which statement describes the circuit immediately after the switch closes?
choices: The current is zero, and the potential difference across the capacitor is \(\varepsilon\).
The current is \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\), and the potential difference across the capacitor is \(\varepsilon\).
The current is zero, because no charge can cross the gap between the capacitor plates.
The current is \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\), and the potential difference across the capacitor is zero.
questions.explanation: An uncharged capacitor has no voltage across it, so at first the full emf appears across the resistor. Charge does not cross the gap, but it flows onto one plate and off the other, so current flows in the circuit.

questions.stem: A long time after the switch in the circuit shown is closed, which statement describes the circuit?
choices: The current is zero, and the potential difference across the capacitor equals \(\varepsilon\).
The current is \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\), and the capacitor is fully charged.
The current is zero, and the capacitor is uncharged.
The current is \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2R}\), and the capacitor has half its final charge.
questions.explanation: As the capacitor charges, its voltage rises and opposes the battery. Current stops when the capacitor's voltage equals the emf, leaving no voltage across the resistor.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, \(\varepsilon=9.0\text{ V}\), \(R=3.0\text{ k}\Omega\), and \(C=10\text{ }\mu\text{F}\). What is the charge on the capacitor a long time after the switch is closed?
questions.explanation: The capacitor charges until its voltage is \(9.0\text{ V}\), so \(Q=CV=(10\times 10^{-6})(9.0)=90\text{ }\mu\text{C}\). The resistance affects how long charging takes, not the final charge.

questions.explanation: With the uncharged capacitor acting like a wire, \(I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{9.0}{3000}=3.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ A}\). Forgetting the kilo prefix gives \(3.0\text{ A}\).

questions.stem: The battery shown has an emf of \(12\text{ V}\) and an internal resistance of \(1.0\text{ }\Omega\), and it is connected to a \(5.0\text{ }\Omega\) resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter read?
questions.explanation: The current is \(\dfrac{12}{1.0+5.0}=2.0\text{ A}\), and the terminal voltage is \(\varepsilon-Ir=12-2.0=10\text{ V}\). The battery's own resistance uses up \(2.0\text{ V}\).

questions.stem: The external resistor in the circuit shown is replaced by one with a smaller resistance. How does the voltmeter reading change?
choices: It increases, because more current flows.
It decreases, because the larger current causes a larger voltage drop across the internal resistance.
It stays at \(12\text{ V}\), because the emf does not change.
It stays the same, because the voltmeter measures the emf.
questions.explanation: The terminal voltage is \(\varepsilon-Ir\). A smaller external resistance draws more current, so more of the emf is lost inside the battery.

questions.stem: A wire of resistance \(R\) is replaced by a wire of the same material that is twice as long and has twice the diameter. What is the resistance of the new wire?
questions.explanation: \(R=\dfrac{\rho L}{A}\). Doubling the length doubles the resistance, and doubling the diameter quadruples the cross-sectional area, which divides the resistance by 4.

questions.stem: A wire of resistance \(R\) is cut into two equal pieces, which are then connected side by side in parallel. What is the resistance of the combination?
questions.explanation: Each half has resistance \(\dfrac{R}{2}\). Two equal resistances in parallel have half the resistance of one, so the combination is \(\dfrac{R}{4}\).

questions.stem: A \(12\text{ V}\) battery and a \(4.0\text{ V}\) battery are connected in a single loop with a \(2.0\text{ }\Omega\) resistor, with their positive terminals facing each other so that they push current in opposite directions. Neglecting internal resistance, what is the current?
questions.explanation: Around the loop the emfs oppose, so the net emf is \(12-4.0=8.0\text{ V}\) and \(I=\dfrac{8.0}{2.0}=4.0\text{ A}\). The smaller battery is being charged.

questions.stem: A student connects an ammeter in parallel with a light bulb instead of in series. What is the likely result?
choices: The ammeter correctly reads the bulb's current.
The bulb becomes brighter, because the ammeter adds current.
Nothing changes, because ammeters have very large resistance.
The bulb goes out, because the ammeter's very small resistance carries nearly all of the current around it.
questions.explanation: An ammeter is designed with a very small resistance so that it barely affects the current when placed in series. In parallel it acts almost like a wire, shorting out the bulb and possibly drawing a dangerously large current.

questions.stem: Why are household outlets wired in parallel rather than in series?
choices: Parallel wiring uses less total current.
Each device receives the full supply voltage and can be switched on or off independently.
Parallel wiring makes the total resistance of the house larger.
In series, each device would receive more voltage than it needs.
questions.explanation: Every branch of a parallel circuit has the same voltage across it. In series, turning one device off would break the circuit for all, and the voltage would be shared among the devices.

questions.stem: A light bulb is rated at \(60\text{ W}\) when connected to \(120\text{ V}\). What is its resistance while operating?
questions.explanation: \(P=\dfrac{V^2}{R}\), so \(R=\dfrac{(120)^2}{60}=240\text{ }\Omega\). The value \(2.0\) is \(\dfrac{V}{P}\), which has no physical meaning here.

questions.stem: A \(60\text{ W}\) bulb and a \(100\text{ W}\) bulb, both rated for \(120\text{ V}\), are connected in series to a \(120\text{ V}\) supply. Which bulb glows brighter?
choices: The \(100\text{ W}\) bulb, because it has the higher power rating
They are equally bright, because they carry the same current
Neither glows, because the voltage is split between them
The \(60\text{ W}\) bulb, because it has the greater resistance and the bulbs carry the same current
questions.explanation: From \(R=\dfrac{V^2}{P}\), the \(60\text{ W}\) bulb has the larger resistance. In series both carry the same current, so the power \(I^2R\) is greater in the bulb with more resistance.

questions.stem: A \(1.5\text{ kW}\) heater runs for \(4.0\text{ h}\). How much electrical energy does it use, in joules?
questions.explanation: The energy is \(Pt=(1500\text{ W})(4.0\times 3600\text{ s})\approx 2.2\times 10^7\text{ J}\), or \(6.0\text{ kWh}\).

questions.stem: Two \(6.0\text{ }\Omega\) resistors are connected in parallel, and the combination is connected in series with a third \(6.0\text{ }\Omega\) resistor. What is the equivalent resistance?
questions.explanation: The parallel pair is \(3.0\text{ }\Omega\), and adding the series resistor gives \(9.0\text{ }\Omega\). All three in series would be \(18\) and all three in parallel \(2.0\).

questions.stem: A student says that current is smaller after it passes through a resistor because the resistor uses some of it up. Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
choices: It is correct: each resistor absorbs some of the charge.
It is correct only for large resistances.
It is incorrect: the current becomes larger after a resistor.
It is incorrect: the current is the same at every point in a series loop, and the resistor converts electrical potential energy, not charge.
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved and does not accumulate in a resistor, so the same current enters and leaves it. What decreases across a resistor is the electric potential, as energy is transferred to thermal energy.

questions.stem: A current of \(2.0\text{ A}\) flows through a wire for \(30\text{ s}\). How many electrons pass a point in the wire? Use \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
questions.explanation: The charge is \(It=60\text{ C}\), and dividing by the charge of one electron gives about \(3.8\times 10^{20}\) electrons.

questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ k}\Omega\) resistor and an \(8.0\text{ k}\Omega\) resistor are connected in series across a \(10\text{ V}\) battery. What is the potential difference across the \(8.0\text{ k}\Omega\) resistor?
questions.explanation: The current is \(\dfrac{10}{10\times 10^3}=1.0\text{ mA}\), so the voltage across the larger resistor is \((1.0\times 10^{-3})(8.0\times 10^3)=8.0\text{ V}\). In series, voltage divides in proportion to resistance.

questions.stem: A resistor is added in parallel to one already connected across an ideal battery. How do the equivalent resistance and the current from the battery change?
choices: The equivalent resistance decreases and the battery current increases.
The equivalent resistance increases and the battery current decreases.
Neither changes, because the original resistor is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Each parallel branch provides another path for charge, so the combined resistance is less than any branch alone. With the same voltage, the battery supplies more current, while the current in the original resistor is unchanged.

questions.stem: A \(6.0\text{ V}\) battery charges a capacitor through a \(2.0\text{ k}\Omega\) resistor. What is the current at the instant the potential difference across the capacitor is \(4.0\text{ V}\)?
questions.explanation: The loop rule gives a resistor voltage of \(6.0-4.0=2.0\text{ V}\), so \(I=\dfrac{2.0}{2000}=1.0\text{ mA}\). The current decreases as the capacitor charges.

questions.stem: In a charging RC circuit, the resistor is replaced with one of greater resistance, and the battery and capacitor are unchanged. How does the process change?
choices: The capacitor charges more slowly but reaches the same final charge.
The capacitor charges faster and reaches a greater final charge.
The capacitor reaches a smaller final charge in the same time.
Nothing changes, because the capacitor determines the charging rate.
questions.explanation: The time constant \(RC\) grows with resistance, so the current is smaller and charging takes longer. The final charge, \(C\varepsilon\), depends only on the capacitance and the emf.

questions.stem: A \(4.0\text{ }\Omega\) resistor and a \(12\text{ }\Omega\) resistor are connected in parallel across a \(6.0\text{ V}\) battery. What is the total current from the battery?
questions.explanation: The branches carry \(\dfrac{6.0}{4.0}=1.5\text{ A}\) and \(\dfrac{6.0}{12}=0.50\text{ A}\), for a total of \(2.0\text{ A}\). Equivalently, the parallel resistance is \(3.0\text{ }\Omega\).

questions.stem: A proton enters the field region shown at \(2.0\times 10^6\text{ m/s}\), perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of \(0.10\text{ T}\). What is the radius of its circular path? Use \(m_p=1.67\times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\) and \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
questions.explanation: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, \(qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}=\dfrac{(1.67\times 10^{-27})(2.0\times 10^6)}{(1.6\times 10^{-19})(0.10)}\approx 0.21\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: In what direction is the magnetic force on the positive particle shown at the instant it enters the field?
choices: Toward the bottom of the page
Toward the top of the page
To the right, in the direction of its velocity
questions.explanation: The force is \(q\vec v\times\vec B\). With \(\vec v\) to the right and \(\vec B\) into the page, the right-hand rule gives a force toward the top of the page. A negative charge would be pushed toward the bottom.

questions.stem: As the particle shown moves through the uniform magnetic field, how does its speed change?
choices: It increases, because the field accelerates the particle.
It decreases, because the field slows the particle.
It increases at first and then decreases.
It stays constant, because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and does no work.
questions.explanation: A force perpendicular to the velocity changes only the direction of motion. The magnetic force does no work, so the particle's kinetic energy and speed stay constant as it follows a circular arc.

questions.stem: An electron enters the field shown with the same velocity as a proton. How does the radius of the electron's path compare with the proton's? \((m_p\approx 1836\,m_e)\)
choices: It is about \(\dfrac{1}{1836}\) as large, and the electron curves in the opposite direction.
It is the same, because the charges have the same magnitude.
It is 1836 times larger, and the electron curves in the same direction.
It is about \(\dfrac{1}{1836}\) as large, and the electron curves in the same direction.
questions.explanation: From \(r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}\), with equal speeds and charge magnitudes the radius is proportional to mass. The electron's negative charge reverses the direction of the force.

questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ m}\) length of wire carrying \(3.0\text{ A}\) lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of \(0.50\text{ T}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the wire?
questions.explanation: \(F=ILB\sin 90^\circ=(3.0)(2.0)(0.50)=3.0\text{ N}\). The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel; dropping the factor of the length gives \(1.5\text{ N}\).

questions.stem: The two wires shown carry currents in the same direction. Which statement describes the magnetic forces between them?
choices: They repel each other with forces of equal magnitude.
They attract each other, and the force on each depends on its own current only.
They attract each other with forces of equal magnitude.
They exert no forces on each other, because the currents are parallel.
questions.explanation: Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other, and the right-hand rules give a force on each directed toward the other. By Newton's third law, the forces are equal and opposite. Antiparallel currents repel.

questions.stem: What is the magnitude of the magnetic force per meter of length that each wire shown exerts on the other? Use \(\mu_0=4\pi\times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\).
questions.explanation: The field from one wire at the other is \(1.0\times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\), so the force per length is \(IB=(5.0)(1.0\times 10^{-5})=5.0\times 10^{-5}\text{ N/m}\).

questions.stem: A long, straight wire carries current directly out of the page. Viewed from above the page, what is the direction of the magnetic field around it?
choices: Counterclockwise circles centered on the wire
Clockwise circles centered on the wire
Straight lines pointing away from the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
questions.explanation: By the right-hand rule, with the thumb along the current, out of the page, the fingers curl counterclockwise. The field lines form closed circles around the wire.

questions.stem: A loop of area \(0.020\text{ m}^2\) is in a uniform magnetic field of \(0.50\text{ T}\) that makes an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the line perpendicular to the plane of the loop. What is the magnetic flux through the loop?
questions.explanation: \(\Phi=BA\cos 60^\circ=(0.50)(0.020)(0.50)=5.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ Wb}\). Only the component of the field perpendicular to the loop contributes; using \(\sin 60^\circ\) gives \(8.7\times 10^{-3}\).

questions.stem: The square loop shown moves at \(2.0\text{ m/s}\) and is entering a field of \(0.40\text{ T}\). What emf is induced in the loop while it is partly inside the field?
questions.explanation: The flux increases at the rate \(BLv\), so the emf is \((0.40)(0.10)(2.0)=0.080\text{ V}\). Only the leading edge, which is inside the field, cuts field lines.

questions.stem: As the loop shown enters the field, what is the direction of the induced current in the loop?
choices: There is no current until the loop is fully inside the field.
It alternates direction as the loop enters.
questions.explanation: The flux into the page is increasing. The induced current opposes that change by producing a field out of the page inside the loop, which requires a counterclockwise current.

questions.stem: Once the loop shown is completely inside the uniform field and still moving to the right, what is the induced current?
choices: The same as while it was entering
Zero, because the flux through the loop is no longer changing
Clockwise, because the loop is leaving its starting position
Larger, because more of the loop is in the field
questions.explanation: An emf is induced only when the magnetic flux changes. Inside a uniform field, the flux stays constant even though the loop moves, so there is no current until the loop begins to leave.

questions.skill: Magnetic force on an induced current

questions.stem: The loop shown has a resistance of \(0.40\text{ }\Omega\), so a current of \(0.20\text{ A}\) is induced as it enters the \(0.40\text{ T}\) field. What external force is needed to keep it moving at constant speed?
choices: None, because the loop moves at constant speed
questions.explanation: The magnetic force on the leading edge is \(ILB=(0.20)(0.10)(0.40)=8.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}\), directed to the left, opposing the motion. An equal force to the right keeps the velocity constant.

questions.explanation: The emf is \(BLv=(0.80)(0.50)(3.0)=1.2\text{ V}\), and the current is \(\dfrac{1.2}{2.0}=0.60\text{ A}\).

questions.stem: As the rod shown slides to the right, what is the direction of the magnetic force on it due to the induced current?
choices: To the left, opposing its motion
To the right, in the direction of motion
Into the page, along the field
There is no force, because the field does no work
questions.explanation: By Lenz's law, the induced current opposes the change that causes it, which here is the rod's motion. If the force pushed the rod forward, it would speed up and create energy from nothing.

questions.stem: The rod shown moves at \(3.0\text{ m/s}\) through a \(0.80\text{ T}\) field with \(R=2.0\text{ }\Omega\), and the current is \(0.60\text{ A}\). At what rate is energy dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: \(P=I^2R=(0.60)^2(2.0)=0.72\text{ W}\). This equals the mechanical power \(Fv=(ILB)v=(0.24)(3.0)\) that must be supplied to keep the rod moving.

questions.stem: The magnetic flux through each turn of a 50-turn coil changes by \(0.020\text{ Wb}\) in \(0.10\text{ s}\). What is the magnitude of the average induced emf?
questions.explanation: \(|\varepsilon|=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=50\left(\dfrac{0.020}{0.10}\right)=10\text{ V}\). Each turn contributes the same emf, so the turns multiply the result.

questions.stem: As the north pole of the magnet shown is pushed toward the coil, what is the magnetic polarity of the end of the coil facing the magnet?
choices: South, so that the coil attracts the magnet
It has no polarity, because the current is too small
North, so that the coil repels the approaching magnet
It alternates rapidly between north and south
questions.explanation: The induced current creates a field that opposes the increase in flux toward the coil, which makes the near end a north pole. The coil therefore pushes back on the magnet, and work must be done to move it closer.

questions.stem: The magnet shown is pushed into the coil and then held at rest inside it. What does the galvanometer show while the magnet is at rest?
choices: A steady current in the same direction as before
A current that increases with time
A steady current in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: A current is induced only while the flux through the coil is changing. A stationary magnet produces a constant flux, so the current stops; it reverses direction when the magnet is pulled out.

questions.stem: The north pole of a compass needle points approximately toward Earth's geographic North Pole. Which statement is correct?
choices: A magnetic south pole lies near Earth's geographic North Pole.
A magnetic north pole lies near Earth's geographic North Pole.
Earth has no magnetic poles; the needle follows electric currents in the air.
The needle points north because north poles attract each other.
questions.explanation: Opposite magnetic poles attract, so the needle's north pole is drawn toward a magnetic south pole. Earth's magnetic field lines point roughly northward at the surface and enter the planet near the geographic North Pole.

questions.stem: A bar magnet is cut in half between its north and south poles. Which describes the two pieces?
choices: One piece is a north pole and the other is a south pole.
Each piece is a complete magnet with its own north and south poles.
One piece keeps both poles and the other loses its magnetism.
questions.explanation: Magnetic poles always occur in pairs; no isolated magnetic pole has ever been observed. The magnetism comes from aligned atomic magnetic moments throughout the material, so each piece is itself a dipole.

questions.stem: In a region with an electric field of \(2000\text{ V/m}\) and a perpendicular magnetic field of \(0.010\text{ T}\), charged particles with one particular speed pass straight through. What is that speed?
questions.explanation: The particle goes straight when the electric and magnetic forces balance, \(qE=qvB\), so \(v=\dfrac{E}{B}=2.0\times 10^5\text{ m/s}\), independent of the charge and mass.

questions.stem: A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on it?
questions.explanation: The magnetic force has magnitude \(qvB\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the velocity and the field. For parallel motion \(\sin\theta=0\), so the particle continues in a straight line.

questions.skill: Circular motion in a magnetic field
questions.stem: What is the period of the circular motion of a proton in a uniform magnetic field of \(0.50\text{ T}\)? Use \(m_p=1.67\times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\) and \(e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
choices: It cannot be determined without the proton's speed.
questions.explanation: The period is \(T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}=\dfrac{2\pi(1.67\times 10^{-27})}{(1.6\times 10^{-19})(0.50)}\approx 1.3\times 10^{-7}\text{ s}\). The speed cancels: faster protons move in larger circles in the same time.

questions.skill: Circular motion in a magnetic field
questions.stem: Two protons with different speeds move in circles in the same uniform magnetic field. How do their periods compare?
choices: The faster proton has the shorter period.
They are equal, because the faster proton moves in a proportionally larger circle.
The faster proton has the longer period.
The periods depend on the direction of motion.
questions.explanation: The radius \(\dfrac{mv}{qB}\) is proportional to speed, so the circumference and the speed grow together and the time per revolution is the same. Cyclotrons rely on this.

questions.skill: Magnetic force on a moving charge
questions.stem: A \(2.0\text{ }\mu\text{C}\) charge moves at \(300\text{ m/s}\) through a \(0.50\text{ T}\) magnetic field, at an angle of \(30^\circ\) to the field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it?
A copper plate swinging as a pendulum passes between the poles of a strong magnet and slows down quickly, though copper is not attracted to a magnet. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The changing flux through the plate induces swirling currents, and the magnetic forces on them oppose the plate's motion.
The magnet attracts the copper, pulling it to a stop.
Air resistance is much greater near a magnet.
The magnet removes electrons from the plate, making it lighter.
questions.explanation: As the plate enters and leaves the field, the flux through parts of it changes and induces eddy currents. By Lenz's law these currents experience forces that oppose the motion, converting kinetic energy into thermal energy. Magnetic braking on trains works this way.

questions.skill: Magnetic field of a current loop
questions.stem: A circular loop of wire carries a steady current. Which statement describes its magnetic field?
choices: It is zero everywhere, because the field from each side of the loop cancels.
It forms circles in the plane of the loop.
It resembles the field of a bar magnet, with one face of the loop acting as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
It points radially outward from the center of the loop.
questions.explanation: Inside the loop the fields from every part of the wire point the same way, through the loop. Field lines emerge from one face and return around the outside to the other, the pattern of a magnetic dipole.

questions.stem: Light in air strikes the glass surface shown at an angle of incidence of \(30^\circ\). What is the angle of refraction in the glass?
questions.explanation: Snell's law gives \(\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{n_1\sin\theta_1}{n_2}=\dfrac{(1.00)(0.50)}{1.50}=0.333\), so \(\theta_2\approx 19.5^\circ\). Light bends toward the normal on entering the denser medium; inverting the ratio gives \(48.6^\circ\).

questions.stem: As the light shown passes from air into the glass, how do its frequency, speed, and wavelength change?
choices: The frequency decreases, the speed decreases, and the wavelength stays the same.
The frequency stays the same, while the speed and the wavelength both decrease.
The speed decreases, and the frequency and the wavelength increase.
questions.explanation: The frequency is set by the source and cannot change at a boundary, or crests would pile up there. The speed drops by a factor of \(n\), and since \(v=f\lambda\), the wavelength drops by the same factor.

questions.skill: Speed of light in a medium
questions.stem: What is the speed of light in glass with an index of refraction of \(1.50\)? Use \(c=3.00\times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
questions.explanation: \(v=\dfrac{c}{n}=\dfrac{3.00\times 10^8}{1.50}=2.00\times 10^8\text{ m/s}\). Light always travels more slowly in a material than in vacuum.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light traveling from the glass shown into air?
questions.explanation: At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, so \(n_1\sin\theta_c=n_2\sin 90^\circ\) and \(\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{1.00}{1.50}\), giving \(\theta_c\approx 41.8^\circ\).

questions.stem: The ray shown strikes the glass–air boundary at an angle of incidence of \(50^\circ\). What happens to it?
choices: It refracts into the air, bending away from the normal.
It refracts into the air, bending toward the normal.
All of it is reflected back into the glass, because the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
It travels along the boundary between the glass and the air.
questions.explanation: The critical angle for glass of index 1.50 is about \(41.8^\circ\). At any larger angle of incidence, Snell's law would require \(\sin\theta_2>1\), which is impossible, so no light is transmitted.

questions.stem: An optical fiber has a glass core surrounded by a cladding layer. Which condition is necessary for light to be trapped in the core by total internal reflection?
choices: The core must have a greater index of refraction than the cladding.
The cladding must have a greater index of refraction than the core.
The core and the cladding must have the same index of refraction.
The light must enter the fiber along the normal to its surface.
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection occurs only when light travels toward a medium with a smaller index of refraction, at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

questions.stem: The object shown is \(30\text{ cm}\) from a converging lens with a focal length of \(10\text{ cm}\). Where is the image?
choices: \(15\text{ cm}\) from the lens, on the same side as the object
\(20\text{ cm}\) from the lens, on the side opposite the object
\(7.5\text{ cm}\) from the lens, on the side opposite the object
\(15\text{ cm}\) from the lens, on the side opposite the object
questions.explanation: The thin-lens equation gives \(\dfrac{1}{d_i}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{2}{30}\), so \(d_i=15\text{ cm}\). The positive value means a real image on the far side of the lens.

questions.stem: The object shown is \(4.0\text{ cm}\) tall, and its image forms \(15\text{ cm}\) from the lens. What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation: The magnification is \(M=-\dfrac{d_i}{d_o}=-\dfrac{15}{30}=-0.50\), so the image is \(0.50(4.0)=2.0\text{ cm}\) tall. The negative sign indicates that it is inverted.

questions.stem: Which describes the image formed in the ray diagram shown?
choices: Virtual, upright, and larger than the object
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object
Real, upright, and smaller than the object
Virtual, inverted, and the same size as the object
questions.explanation: The rays actually meet on the far side of the lens, so the image is real and could be projected on a screen. It lies below the axis, so it is inverted, and it is half the object's height.

questions.stem: The object shown is moved to a point \(5\text{ cm}\) from the lens, inside its focal length. Which describes the new image?
choices: Real, inverted, enlarged, and on the opposite side of the lens
Real, upright, and reduced, on the opposite side of the lens
No image forms, because the object is inside the focal length
Virtual, upright, enlarged, and on the same side of the lens as the object
questions.explanation: Inside the focal length, refracted rays diverge, and they appear to come from a point behind the object. The lens equation gives \(d_i=-10\text{ cm}\) and \(M=+2\): a magnifying glass.

questions.stem: The lower half of the lens shown is covered with black paper. What happens to the image?
choices: The whole image still forms, but it is dimmer.
Only the upper half of the image forms.
Only the lower half of the image forms.
questions.explanation: Every part of the lens receives light from every point of the object. Blocking half of the lens blocks half of the light from each point, so the complete image forms with less brightness.

questions.stem: The object shown is \(15\text{ cm}\) in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of \(10\text{ cm}\). Where is the image, and what is the magnification?
choices: \(30\text{ cm}\) behind the mirror, with a magnification of \(+2\)
\(6.0\text{ cm}\) in front of the mirror, with a magnification of \(-0.4\)
\(30\text{ cm}\) in front of the mirror, with a magnification of \(-2\)
\(25\text{ cm}\) in front of the mirror, with a magnification of \(-1.7\)
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{1}{d_i}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{15}=\dfrac{1}{30}\), so \(d_i=30\text{ cm}\), a real image in front of the mirror, and \(M=-\dfrac{30}{15}=-2\).

questions.stem: An object is placed \(10\text{ cm}\) in front of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is \(40\text{ cm}\). What are the image distance and the magnification?
questions.explanation: The focal length is half the radius, \(20\text{ cm}\). Then \(\dfrac{1}{d_i}=\dfrac{1}{20}-\dfrac{1}{10}=-\dfrac{1}{20}\), so \(d_i=-20\text{ cm}\): a virtual, upright image twice as tall, as in a makeup mirror.

questions.stem: A person walks toward a plane mirror at \(1.0\text{ m/s}\). At what rate does the person approach their own image?
questions.explanation: The image is always as far behind the mirror as the person is in front of it. Both distances shrink at \(1.0\text{ m/s}\), so the distance between them shrinks at \(2.0\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: Why are convex mirrors used as security mirrors in stores?
choices: They always form enlarged images, so that small details are visible.
They always form upright, reduced, virtual images, which show a wide field of view.
They form real images, which can be projected on screens.
They form inverted images, which are easier to interpret.
questions.explanation: A diverging mirror spreads reflected rays, so for any object position the image is virtual, upright, and smaller. Shrinking the image lets a wide area fit in the mirror.

questions.stem: An object is \(30\text{ cm}\) from a diverging lens with a focal length of \(-15\text{ cm}\). What are the image distance and the magnification?
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{1}{d_i}=-\dfrac{1}{15}-\dfrac{1}{30}=-\dfrac{3}{30}\), so \(d_i=-10\text{ cm}\), and \(M=-\dfrac{-10}{30}=+\tfrac{1}{3}\). A diverging lens alone always gives a virtual, upright, reduced image.

questions.stem: A glass lens with an index of refraction of \(1.50\) is moved from air into water, which has an index of \(1.33\). How does its focal length change?
choices: It decreases, because water slows light.
It stays the same, because the focal length depends only on the lens's shape.
It increases, because light bends less at the surfaces when the indices are closer together.
questions.explanation: Refraction at each surface depends on the difference between the indices of the lens and its surroundings. In water that difference is smaller, so the lens bends light less and focuses farther away; it would diverge only if the surroundings had the greater index.

questions.stem: Light in water, with an index of refraction of \(1.33\), strikes a flat glass surface, with an index of \(1.50\), at an angle of incidence of \(40^\circ\). What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: \(\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{1.33\sin 40^\circ}{1.50}=\dfrac{1.33(0.643)}{1.50}\approx 0.570\), so \(\theta_2\approx 35^\circ\). The light bends toward the normal because it enters a medium with a greater index.

questions.stem: White light passing through a glass prism separates into colors, with violet light bending more than red light. What causes this?
choices: The prism adds color to the white light.
Violet light travels faster in glass than red light.
Red light reflects inside the prism, but violet light does not.
The index of refraction of glass is slightly greater for violet light than for red light.
questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because the index of refraction depends on wavelength. Shorter wavelengths, such as violet, travel more slowly in glass and refract through larger angles.

questions.stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror, making an angle of \(35^\circ\) with the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: Angles in optics are measured from the normal. The angle of incidence is \(90^\circ-35^\circ=55^\circ\), and the angle of reflection equals it.

questions.stem: Two plane mirrors meet at a right angle. A ray reflects off one mirror and then off the other. Which describes the final ray?
choices: It travels in the same direction as the incoming ray.
It travels parallel to the incoming ray, in the opposite direction.
It is perpendicular to the incoming ray.
Its direction depends on where it strikes the first mirror.
questions.explanation: Two reflections from perpendicular mirrors reverse the ray's component along each mirror's normal, sending it back antiparallel. Corner reflectors on bicycles and on the Moon use this property.

questions.stem: An object is \(24\text{ cm}\) from a converging lens with a focal length of \(12\text{ cm}\). Which describes the image?
choices: It is \(12\text{ cm}\) from the lens, inverted, and half the size of the object.
It is \(24\text{ cm}\) from the lens, upright, and the same size as the object.
It is \(24\text{ cm}\) from the lens, inverted, and the same size as the object.
questions.explanation: With the object at \(2f\), the lens equation gives \(d_i=24\text{ cm}\) and \(M=-1\). An object at the focal point would form an image at infinity.

questions.stem: An object starts far from a converging lens and moves toward the lens, stopping just outside the focal point. How does its real image change?
choices: It moves farther from the lens and becomes larger.
It moves closer to the lens and becomes smaller.
It moves closer to the lens and becomes larger.
It stays at the focal point and becomes larger.
questions.explanation: A very distant object forms a small image near the focal point. As the object nears \(f\), \(d_i\) grows without bound, and the magnification \(\dfrac{d_i}{d_o}\) grows with it.

questions.stem: An object is \(20\text{ cm}\) from a converging lens, and a real image forms \(60\text{ cm}\) beyond the lens. What is the focal length of the lens?
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{20}+\dfrac{1}{60}=\dfrac{4}{60}\), so \(f=15\text{ cm}\). The magnification is \(-3\).

questions.stem: A straw in a glass of water appears bent at the water's surface. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Light from the submerged part bends toward the normal as it leaves the water.
Water magnifies objects by reflecting light.
The straw actually bends because of water pressure.
Light from the submerged part bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so it appears to come from a point higher than the straw's actual position.
questions.explanation: Rays traveling from water into air refract away from the normal. The eye traces them back in straight lines, so the submerged part of the straw appears raised and the straw seems bent.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light going from diamond, with an index of refraction of \(2.42\), into air?
questions.explanation: \(\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{1}{2.42}\approx 0.413\), so \(\theta_c\approx 24^\circ\). The small critical angle traps light inside a cut diamond through many internal reflections, which makes it sparkle.

questions.stem: The glass shown is replaced by a material with a greater index of refraction, and the angle of incidence is unchanged. How does the refracted ray change?
choices: It bends farther from the normal.
It bends closer to the normal.
It does not change, because the angle of incidence is the same.
questions.explanation: Snell's law gives \(\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{n_2}\), so a larger \(n_2\) makes \(\theta_2\) smaller. Total internal reflection cannot happen for light entering a medium with a greater index.

questions.stem: Light with a wavelength of \(600\text{ nm}\) in air enters glass with an index of refraction of \(1.50\). What is its wavelength in the glass?
questions.explanation: The frequency stays the same while the speed is divided by \(n\), so \(\lambda=\dfrac{600}{1.50}=400\text{ nm}\).

figure.alt: Snapshot of a sinusoidal wave on a string traveling to the right. The displacement y is plotted against position x from 0 to 0.80 m. The amplitude is 5 cm and the wave repeats every 0.40 m. Point P is at a crest at x = 0.10 m, and point Q is at zero displacement at x = 0.20 m

questions.stem: The wave shown has a frequency of \(5.0\text{ Hz}\). What is its speed?
questions.explanation: The pattern repeats every \(0.40\text{ m}\), so \(\lambda=0.40\text{ m}\) and \(v=f\lambda=(5.0)(0.40)=2.0\text{ m/s}\). Reading the length of the whole graph as the wavelength gives \(4.0\text{ m/s}\).

figure.alt: Snapshot of a sinusoidal wave on a string traveling to the right. The displacement y is plotted against position x from 0 to 0.80 m. The amplitude is 5 cm and the wave repeats every 0.40 m. Point P is at a crest at x = 0.10 m, and point Q is at zero displacement at x = 0.20 m

questions.stem: The wave shown travels to the right. At the instant shown, in which direction is the string at point Q moving?
questions.explanation: As the wave moves right, the crest at P will soon arrive at Q's position, so Q must be rising. Points on a transverse wave move perpendicular to the wave's direction, and Q, at zero displacement, has its greatest speed.

questions.stem: The frequency of a wave generator attached to a stretched string is doubled, and the tension is unchanged. How do the speed and wavelength of the waves change?
choices: The speed doubles, and the wavelength stays the same.
The speed and the wavelength both double.
The speed is halved, and the wavelength stays the same.
The speed stays the same, and the wavelength is halved.
questions.explanation: The speed of a wave on a string depends only on the tension and the mass per unit length. With \(v\) fixed, \(\lambda=\dfrac{v}{f}\) is halved.

questions.stem: The tension in a string is quadrupled. By what factor does the speed of waves on the string change?
choices: It increases by a factor of 16.
questions.explanation: The wave speed is \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{F_T}{\mu}}\), so multiplying the tension by 4 multiplies the speed by \(\sqrt{4}=2\).

figure.alt: A standing wave on a string 1.2 m long fixed at both ends. The pattern has three loops, with nodes at both ends and two nodes between them

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of the standing wave shown?
questions.explanation: Each loop is half a wavelength. Three loops span \(1.2\text{ m}\), so \(\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda=1.2\text{ m}\) and \(\lambda=0.80\text{ m}\). The length of one loop, \(0.40\text{ m}\), is half the wavelength.

figure.alt: A standing wave on a string 1.2 m long fixed at both ends. The pattern has three loops, with nodes at both ends and two nodes between them

questions.stem: Waves travel at \(120\text{ m/s}\) on the string shown. What is the fundamental frequency of the string?
questions.explanation: The fundamental has one loop, so \(\lambda_1=2L=2.4\text{ m}\) and \(f_1=\dfrac{120}{2.4}=50\text{ Hz}\). The pattern shown is the third harmonic, at \(150\text{ Hz}\).

figure.alt: A standing wave on a string 1.2 m long fixed at both ends. The pattern has three loops, with nodes at both ends and two nodes between them

questions.stem: How many nodes and antinodes does the standing wave shown have, counting the fixed ends?
questions.explanation: Nodes lie at both fixed ends and at the two points where the loops meet. Each of the three loops has one antinode at its center, where the string oscillates with the largest amplitude.

questions.stem: The tube shown is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound is \(340\text{ m/s}\). What is the frequency of its lowest resonance?
questions.explanation: The closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode, so the tube holds a quarter wavelength: \(\lambda=4L=3.4\text{ m}\) and \(f=\dfrac{340}{3.4}=100\text{ Hz}\).

questions.stem: Which frequencies can resonate in the tube shown, if its lowest resonant frequency is \(f_1\)?
choices: Only odd multiples of \(f_1\), such as \(3f_1\) and \(5f_1\)
questions.explanation: Each resonance must have a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. That requires an odd number of quarter wavelengths in the tube, so only odd harmonics occur.

questions.stem: A pipe \(0.85\text{ m}\) long is open at both ends, and the speed of sound is \(340\text{ m/s}\). What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.explanation: Both ends are antinodes, so the fundamental is half a wavelength: \(\lambda=2L=1.7\text{ m}\) and \(f=\dfrac{340}{1.7}=200\text{ Hz}\), twice the fundamental of a pipe of the same length closed at one end.

questions.stem: In the setup shown, \(d=0.10\text{ mm}\), \(L=2.0\text{ m}\), and the light has a wavelength of \(600\text{ nm}\). What is the distance on the screen between adjacent bright fringes?
questions.explanation: For small angles, the spacing is \(\Delta y=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}=\dfrac{(600\times 10^{-9})(2.0)}{1.0\times 10^{-4}}=0.012\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: In the setup shown, the slits are moved closer together and everything else is unchanged. How does the fringe pattern change?
questions.explanation: The fringe spacing is \(\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}\), so a smaller slit separation means a larger spacing. Closer slits need a larger angle to produce the same path difference.

questions.stem: Point P in the diagram is at the first bright fringe above the central maximum. How does the distance from P to the lower slit compare with the distance from P to the upper slit?
choices: It is greater by half a wavelength.
It is greater by one wavelength.
It is greater by two wavelengths.
questions.explanation: Bright fringes occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in phase. The central maximum has zero path difference, and a half-wavelength difference gives a dark fringe.

questions.stem: Light with a wavelength of \(500\text{ nm}\) strikes a diffraction grating with \(500\) lines per millimeter. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
questions.explanation: The line spacing is \(d=\dfrac{1}{500}\text{ mm}=2.0\times 10^{-6}\text{ m}\). Then \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{d}=0.25\), and \(\theta\approx 14.5^\circ\).

questions.stem: How does the pattern from a diffraction grating with thousands of slits compare with the pattern from two slits with the same spacing?
choices: The maxima are at larger angles and are broader.
The grating produces only one bright spot.
The bright maxima are at the same angles but are much narrower and brighter.
questions.explanation: The positions of the maxima depend only on the spacing, \(d\sin\theta=m\lambda\). With many slits, waves cancel almost completely except very near those angles, giving sharp, bright lines useful for measuring wavelengths.

questions.stem: A soap film like the one shown has an index of refraction of \(1.33\). What is the smallest nonzero thickness \(t\) for which light with a wavelength of \(532\text{ nm}\) in air strongly reflects?
questions.explanation: Ray 1 is inverted on reflection from the denser film, while ray 2 is not. Constructive interference therefore requires an extra path of half a wavelength in the film: \(2t=\dfrac{\lambda}{2n}\), so \(t=\dfrac{532}{4(1.33)}=100\text{ nm}\).

questions.stem: Just before a soap bubble pops, its film becomes much thinner than the wavelength of visible light, and the film appears black in reflected light. Why?
choices: A very thin film absorbs all of the light.
Only one of the two reflected rays is inverted, so with almost no extra path they cancel for every color.
Both reflected rays are inverted, so they cancel.
The thin film transmits no light.
questions.explanation: With negligible path difference, the only difference between rays 1 and 2 is the half-cycle shift of ray 1 at the denser film. The rays are out of phase for all wavelengths, so little light is reflected.
