questions.stem: The diagram shows sound waves from a moving source. How do the frequencies heard by observers A and B compare with the frequency emitted by the source?
choices: A hears a lower frequency and B hears a higher frequency.
Both hear the emitted frequency, because the speed of sound is constant.
Both hear a higher frequency, because the source is moving.
A hears a higher frequency and B hears a lower frequency.
questions.explanation: The source moves toward A, so the crests reaching A are closer together and arrive more often. Behind the source, at B, the crests are spread apart and arrive less often.

questions.stem: For the moving source shown, how does the speed of the sound waves reaching observer A compare with the speed of the waves reaching observer B?
choices: The waves reaching A are faster.
The waves reaching B are faster.
The waves reaching A are faster by exactly the speed of the source.
questions.explanation: Once emitted, sound travels at a speed set by the air, not by the source. The source's motion changes the spacing of the crests and so the wavelength and frequency, but not the wave speed.

questions.stem: A small speaker radiates sound equally in all directions. A listener moves from \(2.0\text{ m}\) to \(4.0\text{ m}\) from the speaker. By what factor does the sound intensity change?
choices: It is reduced to one eighth.
It is reduced to one quarter.
questions.explanation: The power spreads over a sphere of area \(4\pi r^2\), so intensity is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{r^2}\). Doubling the distance divides it by 4.

questions.stem: A sound wave travels from air into water, in which sound travels about four times as fast. How do its frequency and wavelength change?
choices: The frequency increases, and the wavelength stays the same.
The frequency stays the same, and the wavelength decreases.
The frequency stays the same, and the wavelength increases.
questions.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source and does not change at a boundary. Since \(\lambda=\dfrac{v}{f}\), the wavelength increases in proportion to the speed.

questions.stem: Two tuning forks with frequencies of \(440\text{ Hz}\) and \(444\text{ Hz}\) sound together. What beat frequency is heard?
questions.explanation: The loudness rises and falls at the difference of the two frequencies, \(444-440=4\text{ Hz}\). The tone heard is at the average, \(442\text{ Hz}\).

questions.stem: Which statement explains why sound waves in air cannot be polarized but light waves can?
choices: Sound waves are too slow to be polarized.
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave, and only transverse waves have an oscillation direction that can be restricted.
Sound waves have wavelengths that are too long.
Light waves travel through a medium, and sound waves do not.
questions.explanation: Polarization selects one direction of oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel. A longitudinal wave oscillates only along its direction of travel, so there is nothing to select.

questions.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity \(I_0\) passes through the two polarizers shown. What is the intensity of the light that emerges?
questions.explanation: The first polarizer passes half of unpolarized light. The second passes the fraction \(\cos^2 60^\circ=\tfrac{1}{4}\) of that, by Malus's law, leaving \(\dfrac{I_0}{8}\).

questions.stem: Two pulses of equal shape and size but opposite displacement travel toward each other on a string. At the instant they exactly overlap, the string is straight. Which statement is correct at that instant?
choices: The pulses have destroyed each other, and their energy has been lost.
The pulses have reflected from each other.
The energy of the pulses is still present, as kinetic energy of the moving string.
The string is at rest everywhere.
questions.explanation: Displacements add, so the string is flat, but its velocities do not cancel: the segments are moving fastest. The pulses then pass through each other and continue unchanged.

questions.stem: Light passes through a single narrow slit and forms a pattern on a distant screen. The slit is made narrower. How does the central bright band change?
questions.explanation: The first dark fringes lie at \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\), where \(a\) is the slit width. A narrower slit diffracts light into a wider angle.

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of a radio wave with a frequency of \(100\text{ MHz}\)? Use \(c=3.0\times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
questions.explanation: \(\lambda=\dfrac{c}{f}=\dfrac{3.0\times 10^8}{1.0\times 10^8}=3.0\text{ m}\). All electromagnetic waves travel at \(c\) in vacuum.

questions.stem: A pulse traveling along a string reaches an end that is tied firmly to a wall. Which describes the reflected pulse?
choices: It is upright and travels back along the string.
It is inverted and travels back along the string.
It passes into the wall, and nothing is reflected.
It is inverted and stays at the wall.
questions.explanation: At a fixed end, the string pulls up on the wall, and the wall pulls down on the string. That reaction produces an inverted pulse. A free end reflects the pulse upright.

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen atom moves from \(n=3\) to \(n=2\)? Use \(hc=1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}\).
questions.explanation: The photon energy is \(-1.51-(-3.40)=1.89\text{ eV}\), and \(\lambda=\dfrac{1240}{1.89}\approx 656\text{ nm}\), the red line in the visible hydrogen spectrum.

questions.stem: What is the least energy needed to ionize a hydrogen atom in its ground state?
questions.explanation: Ionization lifts the electron from \(-13.6\text{ eV}\) to \(0\text{ eV}\), where it is no longer bound. The energy \(10.2\text{ eV}\) only raises it to \(n=2\).

questions.stem: A sample of hydrogen atoms is excited to the \(n=4\) level. As the electrons return to the ground state, how many different photon energies can be emitted?
questions.explanation: Any two of the four levels can be connected by a transition: 4 to 3, 2, or 1; 3 to 2 or 1; and 2 to 1. That gives \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) distinct energies.

questions.stem: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are illuminated by photons of \(10.2\text{ eV}\) and photons of \(11.0\text{ eV}\). Which photons are absorbed?
choices: Both kinds, because each has enough energy to reach \(n=2\)
Only the \(11.0\text{ eV}\) photons, because they have more energy
Only the \(10.2\text{ eV}\) photons, because only they match the energy difference between two levels
Neither kind, because both have less than \(13.6\text{ eV}\)
questions.explanation: A photon is absorbed only if its whole energy equals the difference between two levels. No level lies \(11.0\text{ eV}\) above the ground state, so those photons pass through. A colliding electron, by contrast, can give up part of its energy.

questions.stem: What is the longest wavelength of light emitted by hydrogen atoms in transitions that end in the ground state? Use \(hc=1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}\).
questions.explanation: The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest energy, the \(10.2\text{ eV}\) transition from \(n=2\) to \(n=1\): \(\dfrac{1240}{10.2}\approx 122\text{ nm}\), in the ultraviolet. The value \(91\text{ nm}\) is the shortest wavelength, from ionization.

questions.stem: Why are the two lines on the graph parallel?
choices: Both metals have the same work function.
The slope of each line is Planck's constant, which is the same for every metal.
Both metals were illuminated with the same intensity.
The slope is the electron's charge, which is the same for both metals.
questions.explanation: Einstein's equation, \(K_{\max}=hf-\phi\), is a line with slope \(h\) and an intercept set by the work function. Different metals shift the line without changing its slope.

questions.stem: Light with a frequency of \(1.0\times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}\) shines on metal B. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons? Use \(h=4.14\times 10^{-15}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{s}\).
questions.explanation: The threshold of metal B is \(7.0\times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\), so \(K_{\max}=h(f-f_0)=(4.14\times 10^{-15})(3.0\times 10^{14})\approx 1.2\text{ eV}\).

questions.stem: Light with a frequency of \(6.0\times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\) shines on metal B, and no electrons are emitted. The intensity of the light is then greatly increased. What happens?
choices: Electrons are emitted, because more energy reaches the metal.
Electrons are emitted after a delay, once enough energy builds up.
Still no electrons are emitted, because each photon has less energy than the work function.
Electrons are emitted with greater kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Each electron absorbs a single photon, whose energy \(hf\) depends only on frequency. Below the threshold, no single photon can free an electron, however many photons arrive. This result contradicted the classical wave model of light.

questions.stem: Light above the threshold frequency shines on metal A, and its intensity is doubled while its frequency is unchanged. What happens to the photoelectrons?
choices: Twice as many are emitted per second, with the same maximum kinetic energy.
The same number are emitted, with twice the maximum kinetic energy.
Twice as many are emitted, each with twice the maximum kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Doubling intensity at fixed frequency doubles the number of photons, and so the number of electrons freed. Each photon still carries \(hf\), so the maximum kinetic energy is unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of light with a wavelength of \(500\text{ nm}\)? Use \(hc=1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}\).
questions.explanation: \(E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{1240}{500}\approx 2.5\text{ eV}\). Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon.

questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at \(1.0\times 10^6\text{ m/s}\)? Use \(h=6.63\times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\) and \(m_e=9.11\times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\).
questions.explanation: \(\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}=\dfrac{6.63\times 10^{-34}}{(9.11\times 10^{-31})(1.0\times 10^6)}\approx 7.3\times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\), comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal.

questions.stem: A beam of electrons passing through a thin crystal produces a pattern of bright and dark rings on a screen. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Electrons are particles, because they hit the screen at points.
Electrons have wave properties, because the pattern results from interference.
The crystal emits light when struck by electrons.
questions.explanation: Rings of constructive and destructive interference are a signature of waves. The Davisson–Germer experiment confirmed de Broglie's prediction that matter has a wavelength \(\dfrac{h}{p}\).

questions.stem: When an X-ray photon scatters off a nearly free electron, the scattered photon has a longer wavelength than the incident photon. What does this show?
choices: X-rays slow down when they scatter.
The electron emits a second photon of longer wavelength.
Photons carry momentum and energy, and they transfer some of each to the electron in a collision.
questions.explanation: Compton treated the scattering as a particle collision. The electron recoils and gains energy, so the photon's energy \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\) decreases and its wavelength increases.

questions.stem: What is the momentum of a photon with a wavelength of \(663\text{ nm}\)? Use \(h=6.63\times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\).
questions.explanation: \(p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.63\times 10^{-34}}{6.63\times 10^{-7}}=1.0\times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}\). Leaving the wavelength in nanometers gives the second value.

figure.alt: Graph of the number of undecayed nuclei in a radioactive sample versus time. The number starts at 800, falls to 400 at 5 days and to 200 at 10 days, and continues to decrease exponentially toward zero

questions.stem: According to the graph, how many undecayed nuclei remain after \(15\) days?
questions.explanation: The number falls by half every \(5\) days: \(800\) to \(400\) to \(200\) to \(100\) after three half-lives. Dividing \(800\) by the three half-lives gives \(267\), which treats decay as linear.

figure.alt: Graph of the number of undecayed nuclei in a radioactive sample versus time. The number starts at 800, falls to 400 at 5 days and to 200 at 10 days, and continues to decrease exponentially toward zero

questions.stem: For the sample graphed, what fraction of the original nuclei remains after \(20\) days?
questions.explanation: Twenty days is four half-lives, so the fraction is \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^4=\dfrac{1}{16}\), or \(50\) nuclei. The amount approaches zero but never reaches it.

figure.alt: Graph of the number of undecayed nuclei in a radioactive sample versus time. The number starts at 800, falls to 400 at 5 days and to 200 at 10 days, and continues to decrease exponentially toward zero

questions.stem: Which statement about the decay of the sample graphed is correct?
choices: The nuclei decay one after another in a fixed order.
The half-life shortens as fewer nuclei remain.
The probability that any given nucleus decays in the next day is constant, but which nuclei decay cannot be predicted.
All of the nuclei will have decayed after \(10\) days.
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay is random for individual nuclei. Because each nucleus has the same constant chance of decaying per unit time, a large sample decays exponentially with a fixed half-life.

questions.stem: Uranium-238, \(^{238}_{92}\text{U}\), undergoes alpha decay. What is the resulting nucleus?
questions.explanation: An alpha particle, \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\), carries away 4 nucleons and 2 protons. The mass number falls to 234 and the atomic number to 90, which is thorium.

questions.stem: Carbon-14, \(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\), undergoes beta-minus decay. What is the resulting nucleus?
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay, a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted. The mass number stays 14, and the atomic number rises from 6 to 7, which is nitrogen.

questions.stem: Which process occurs inside a nucleus during beta-minus decay?
choices: A proton changes into a neutron, emitting an electron.
An electron orbiting the atom falls into the nucleus.
A neutron changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino.
The nucleus emits a helium nucleus.
questions.explanation: The emitted electron is created in the decay; it was not in the nucleus beforehand. The antineutrino carries away part of the energy, which is why beta electrons have a range of energies.

questions.stem: How much energy is released if \(1.0\text{ g}\) of mass is converted entirely into energy? Use \(c=3.0\times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
questions.explanation: \(E=mc^2=(1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ kg})(3.0\times 10^8)^2=9.0\times 10^{13}\text{ J}\). Using \(1.0\text{ kg}\) instead of grams gives \(9.0\times 10^{16}\text{ J}\).

questions.stem: The mass of a helium-4 nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons by \(0.0304\text{ u}\). What is its binding energy? \((1\text{ u}\) corresponds to \(931.5\text{ MeV})\)
questions.explanation: The mass defect times \(931.5\text{ MeV/u}\) gives \(0.0304(931.5)\approx 28.3\text{ MeV}\). Dividing by the four nucleons gives about \(7.1\text{ MeV}\) per nucleon.

questions.stem: Both the fission of uranium and the fusion of hydrogen release energy. Which statement explains why?
choices: In both, the total number of nucleons decreases.
In both, the products have a greater binding energy per nucleon than the reactants, so their total mass is less.
Fission releases energy, and fusion only absorbs it.
In both, mass is created from energy.
questions.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron. Splitting heavy nuclei or joining light nuclei moves toward that peak, and the decrease in mass appears as released energy, \(\Delta E=\Delta mc^2\).

questions.stem: How does gamma decay change a nucleus?
choices: It lowers the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4.
It lowers the nucleus's energy without changing its atomic number or mass number.
It raises the atomic number by 1.
It changes a proton into a neutron.
questions.explanation: A gamma ray is a high-energy photon emitted as an excited nucleus moves to a lower energy state, much as an atom emits light. Photons carry no charge or nucleons.

questions.stem: Which quantities must be the same before and after every nuclear reaction?
choices: Total number of protons and total number of neutrons separately
Total charge and total number of nucleons
questions.explanation: Charge and nucleon number are always conserved, which is how missing products are identified. Protons and neutrons can convert into each other in beta decay, and rest mass changes as energy is released.

questions.stem: The spectrum of a star peaks at a wavelength of \(500\text{ nm}\). Using Wien's law with \(b=2.9\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\cdot\text{K}\), what is the star's surface temperature?
questions.explanation: Wien's law gives \(T=\dfrac{b}{\lambda_{\max}}=\dfrac{2.9\times 10^{-3}}{5.0\times 10^{-7}}\approx 5800\text{ K}\), close to the Sun's surface temperature.

questions.stem: The temperature of a glowing object is increased. How does its emitted spectrum change?
choices: The peak shifts to longer wavelengths, and less radiation is emitted.
The peak stays fixed, and only the total intensity increases.
The peak shifts to shorter wavelengths, and more radiation is emitted at every wavelength.
The object emits only one wavelength at higher temperatures.
questions.explanation: Hotter objects glow from red toward white and blue. Explaining the shape of this spectrum led Planck to propose that energy is emitted in quanta.
